description: We are a multidisciplinary team from Ghana passionate about AI, robotics, space, Earth observation, software, and emerging technologies. We want to use NASA data to build practical solutions with real-world impact. We welcome teammates skilled in AI/ML, data science, Earth/space science, hardware, UI/UX, design, research, storytelling, and business. Let’s explore the next frontier together!
summary:
Black Star Orbit is an interactive astronomical discovery platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It transforms infrared sky observations into an investigative workspace for exploring moving and variable celestial sources, supporting research relevant to the search for distant objects such as Planet X.

The platform integrates NASA's SPHEREx spectral image data with historical AllWISE observations and ESA's Gaia DR3 astrometric catalogue. Users can search astronomical targets by name or coordinates, explore observations across different survey epochs, compare infrared images, inspect spectral information, and investigate potential changes in source position or brightness.

Its custom FITS-processing pipeline performs image parsing, World Coordinate System alignment, background correction, and difference imaging to support meaningful comparisons across observation dates. Black Star Orbit aims to make complex astronomical datasets more accessible while encouraging transparent, evidence-based scientific investigation. It distinguishes observed signals from unconfirmed candidates and never presents a candidate as a confirmed discovery without sufficient evidence.
details:
Project Black Star Orbit

Overview

Black Star Orbit is an interactive infrared astronomy platform designed to help users investigate celestial objects through observations collected at different points in time. It was developed around the scientific challenge of identifying and investigating possible moving or variable objects in the outer Solar System, including objects relevant to the Planet X search.

Rather than relying on a single image or catalogue entry, the platform brings together observations from multiple astronomical surveys and allows users to investigate how a source changes across observation epochs.


How it works


1. Editorial Journal
You are welcomed with a little documentation and a brief news update on space explorations at your journal :)

2. Astronomical target discovery

Users can search for an astronomical object using its name or celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination). The platform uses these coordinates to retrieve relevant observations and catalogue information.

3. NASA SPHEREx data integration

The platform queries NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive for SPHEREx spectral image observations from Data Release 1 (DR1) and Quick Release 3 (QR3). It retrieves available Level-2 FITS products and their associated observation metadata.

4. Historical infrared comparison

The project incorporates historical AllWISE observations to provide an earlier infrared reference. This enables comparisons between older WISE observations and more recent SPHEREx observations, creating a longer observational baseline.

5. FITS processing and image alignment

A custom TypeScript-based FITS processing pipeline reads astronomical image data and relevant World Coordinate System (WCS) information. It handles image orientation, coordinate transformations and reprojection onto a common North-Up sky grid. The platform also supports background correction, variance-aware signal-to-noise analysis, aperture photometry and difference imaging.

6. Stellar catalogue cross-matching

ESA Gaia DR3 data provides astrometric information, including proper motions and parallaxes. This helps distinguish known stellar motion from signals that may warrant further investigation.

7. Time-machine visualization

Users can browse observations chronologically, compare images using a blink viewer, inspect available spectral information and investigate image differences. The interface also provides tools for examining signal-to-noise information and potential source displacement.

8. Candidate investigation

Potential signals are organized for further examination. The platform distinguishes observed signals, unconfirmed candidates and confirmed discoveries. It does not claim to have discovered Planet X; instead, it provides a transparent environment for investigating evidence.

Technology and tools

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite and modern CSS.

- Backend: Node.js and Express.

- Astronomical data: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx archive, NASA/IPAC AllWISE and ESA Gaia DR3.

- Scientific image processing: FITS parsing, WCS transformations, image reprojection, aperture photometry and difference imaging.

- Infrastructure: Vercel, Render and GitHub version control.

- AI assistance: NVIDIA NIM integration for AI-assisted explanations and astronomical exploration, with deterministic responses available when the external AI service is unavailable.

Creativity and innovation

The main innovation is the integration of multiple astronomical data sources into a single time-domain investigation workflow. Instead of presenting static sky images, Black Star Orbit allows users to compare observations across years, align images despite different spacecraft orientations, examine differences and investigate candidate signals.

The custom FITS-processing pipeline is particularly important because observations taken at different times may have different orientations, calibrations and backgrounds. Aligning them to a common coordinate grid makes comparisons more meaningful.

Benefits and intended impact

Black Star Orbit aims to:

- Make publicly available infrared astronomy data easier to explore.

- Support investigation of moving and variable celestial sources.

- Help users compare observations across different missions and time periods.

- Encourage reproducible, evidence-based astronomical analysis.

- Provide an accessible starting point for students, citizen scientists and astronomy enthusiasts.

Scientific limitations

The platform is an investigative and candidate-triage tool, not an automated discovery authority. Apparent changes can arise from instrumental effects, image alignment errors, background variations, calibration differences or genuine astrophysical variability. Every candidate requires independent validation and, where appropriate, additional observations.

Live archive availability also depends on the operational status of external data services. When real observations cannot be retrieved, the application explicitly identifies simulated fallback content rather than presenting it as NASA data.
